extracted.intended_audience: researchers and scholars in media studies and climate communication; journalists and media analysts interested in climate-change coverage
extracted.subtask_description: Systematic content-analysis and critical-discourse assessment of how national print newspapers represent anthropogenic climate change (2005–2019), including sampling, coding, reliability testing, and statistical comparison to scientific consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Selected 17 national print media sources in five countries that met the criteria of: (a) high circulation and (b) accessibility of the entire article text through the Nexis Uni database in 2019.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes explicit list of sources by country (e.g., Guardian/Observer, Daily Mail/Mail on Sunday, New York Times, USA Today, Washington Post, etc.). Selection rationale: focus on high-circulation national print outlets to enable cross-national comparison in Anglophone contexts where climate contrarianism is concentrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The unit of analysis was the individual article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles include news articles, letters, editorials, and other publications that contained the keywords 'global warming' or 'climate change.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Search terms and Nexis Uni usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles were searched with keywords 'global warming' or 'climate change' using Nexis Uni, and duplicates were not grouped to ensure replicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: Nexis Uni continuously re-groups what they consider duplicates, so explicit decision to not group duplicates supports replicable sampling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Population N = 246,320 articles. A random number generator was used on each month to take an initial 20% sample (N = 48,603). To further randomize selection, 10% of that sample was chronologically analyzed using a random number generator on each month to yield the final sample N = 4,856.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure preserves month-level randomization and replicability; details on percent-sampling at two stages are provided to justify final sample size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion/exclusion into final analytic set
rubrics_metrics.description: Category 5 (not applicable) articles were removed from the final analytic sample. Of the 4,856 coded, 2,194 were Category 5 and removed, yielding N = 2,662 articles directly relevant to causes of climate change for analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category 5 includes articles where climate change mention was peripheral or where the article discussed adaptation without mentioning the science of anthropogenic causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding categories (Category 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Category 1: 'anthropogenic global warming only contributes to climate change (distinct from natural variations)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples provided in Table 3; Category 1 made up negligible percentages across years (only present in a few years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding categories (Category 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Category 2: 'anthropogenic global warming significantly contributes to climate change (in combination with natural variation)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalized as representing the scientific consensus; used as the primary indicator of 'scientifically accurate reporting' in statistical comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding categories (Category 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Category 3: 'anthropogenic global warming and natural variability equally contribute to climate change'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated as 'false balance' — coverage that provides roughly equal attention/emphasis to competing viewpoints and thus misrepresents the scientific consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding categories (Category 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Category 4: 'anthropogenic global warming negligently contributes to climate change' (i.e., articles that refute the existence of climate change or claim it is not driven primarily by humans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represents denialist or contrarian coverage in the coding scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'balance' / false balance
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Balance’ was determined to be coverage that provided roughly equal attention and emphasis to competing viewpoints on anthropogenic climate change, however not necessarily equal time and space (Entman 1989, Dunwoody and Peters 1992, Boykoff 2011).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper treats roughly equal emphasis to contrarian perspectives as informational bias when it misrepresents the weight of scientific consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding approach: critical discourse analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Coding was conducted using a critical discourse analytic approach rather than tallying frequencies of words or phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on combinations of terminology, framing techniques, salience of elements, tone, and relationships among message clusters to discern intertextual patterns. Validity of discourse analysis is described as established when linguistic details converge to support agreement (Gee 2014).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coder procedure and quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Each article was independently coded by two coders in a larger group of six; pairing of coders was rotated once during analysis; coders convened at regular intervals to assess interpretive convergence and update the codebook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coding included iterative refinement of codebook and assembled notes capturing illustrative passages and representative examples from sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intercoder reliability thresholds and metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Intercoder agreement was 89.6%; Krippendorff alpha = 0.81; Scott’s Pi = 0.809, meeting acceptability standards (Lombard et al 2002).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These numeric thresholds are treated as acceptable evidence of coding reliability for the qualitative/quantitative hybrid analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of tone in coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Coders generally coded based on the content of the article itself, as tone can be difficult to interpret; if tone came through strongly in an article, this was reflected in the final category assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizes variability in reader interpretation of sarcasm or mocking tone; the team did not aim for a 'perfect formula' for tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of non-news article types
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters, editorials, and other publications were included because they reflect the overall content of the sources and impact readers, even if outside strict journalistic norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers note these unit types may not follow guidelines on balance/truth in reporting but were retained to reflect source content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical testing and hypothesis framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Null hypothesis: newspaper coverage reflected the convergent agreement in the scientific community regarding anthropogenic climate change (H0: π1 = π2). Alternative: media portrayals significantly diverged (Ha: π1 ≠ π2). Used z-score significance testing (comparing ratios) with conventional z thresholds (z ≥ 1.96 p = 0.05; z ≥ 2.575 p = 0.01; z ≥ 3.29 p = 0.001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Z-score formula provided; primary quantitative comparisons contrast percent Category 2 vs Categories 1+3+4 combined, and compute percent differences and z-scores by year and by source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational metric of accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientifically accurate reporting is operationalized as Category 2 coverage (portraying that humans significantly contribute to observed climate change); analyses report percent of Category 2 articles and percent difference between Category 2 and Categories 1, 3, & 4 combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trend analysis over 2005–2019 focuses on percentage of Category 2 articles as the indicator of improved accuracy over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative/causal limitations and scope notes
rubrics_metrics.description: The study notes that sampling focuses on print newspapers and does not analyze placement, prominence, or other media (cable news, digital-native media, radio), and that causal drivers of variation are outside scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers caution against overgeneralizing results beyond examined outlets, article types, and timeframe; they flag future research directions (e.g., other media formats, prominence metrics, discourses of delay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Replicability and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: An abbreviated codebook is provided in the supplement (full codebook in supplementary materials online). Duplicates were not grouped in Nexis searches to ensure replicability; coders documented notes and illustrative quotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data availability: data supporting findings available upon reasonable request from authors; detailed sampling and coding procedures documented to facilitate replication.
